# The Thermodynamic Complexity of Circuits<sup>∗</sup>

Anne Condon<sup>†</sup><sup>1</sup>, David Doty<sup>‡</sup><sup>2</sup>, Niels Kornerup<sup>§</sup><sup>3</sup>, David Soloveichik\(^\unknown^{4}\), and David Wolpert<sup>‖</sup><sup>5</sup>

<sup>1</sup>University of British Columbia

<sup>2</sup>University of California, Davis

<sup>3</sup>Sandia National Laboratories

<sup>4</sup>University of Texas, Austin

<sup>5</sup>Santa Fe Institute, New Mexico; Complexity Science Hub, Vienna; Arizona State University, Arizona; International Center for Theoretical Physics, Trieste

**Abstract**

When any physical system executes a logically irreversible (non-injective) step of a computation, the excess heat released over the so-called Landauer limit is an energetic cost that cannot be recovered. In modern computers this cost vastly dwarfs the Landauer limit. Modern stochastic thermodynamics refers to this cost as the "entropy production" and has derived some very powerful lower bounds on its value, which strictly strengthen the second law of thermodynamics. Here we introduce a model of circuits using _heat functions_ and investigate its entropy production, deriving new results on the thermodynamic complexity of circuits.

In our model, the circuits compute _cleanly_, erasing their inputs and all intermediate values. We first show that computing the optimal heat functions for gates in a given circuit (the gates that minimize total entropy production) when the circuit’s input is uniformly random is PP-complete. We also show that multiplicative approximation of those heat functions is NP-hard, but additive approximation admits a polynomial-time randomized algorithm. We give tight bounds for entropy production for certain specific families of circuits (on uniformly distributed inputs): an _n_-ary AND tree of depth _O_(log_n_) requires \(\Omega(n)\) circuit entropy production, while a serial chain achieves _O_(1), showing an energy-depth tradeoff. The Batcher odd-even mergesort network on _n_ bits has \(\Theta(n)\) entropy production, asymptotically less than its \(\Theta(nlog^2n)\) gate count. On random permutations of distinct integers its entropy production is \(\Theta(nlog^2n)\), asymptotically exceeding the Landauer cost of sorting; but preceding it with Leighton and Plaxton’s almost-sorting network reduces the total heat released to _O(n_log_n_). Finally, we show that a clean sorting circuit (not a sorting network) can sort _n_ values with zero circuit entropy production over any exchangeable input distribution. Our framework also yields streamlined proofs of known results in stochastic thermodynamics on mismatch cost and modularity cost.

## 1 Introduction

A central part of the industrial revolution of the 19th century was the invention of steam engines. This invention resulted in a practical demand for powerful and efficient steam engines, which in turn ignited a mathematical revolution in physics: the development of the theory of thermodynamics to<tbc>

<tbc>understand and quantify how efficiently an engine could accomplish mechanical objectives such as moving a large train.

Then in the 20th century there was a similarly revolutionary invention, of computers. Accordingly, the energy required to accomplish _computational_ objectives has been a subject of academic inquiry for a century. A deeper and more powerful understanding of this thermodynamics of computation would not just be a purely theoretical advance. As a practical matter, we live in a world where the energetic costs of computing are critically important. The International Energy Agency estimates that 485 terawatt-hours was consumed running data centers in the year 2025 and projects that this number will roughly double to 950 terawatt-hours in 2030 [Int26]. Despite this, our theoretical understanding of the fundamental thermodynamic costs of computation is rather limited, partially due to the lack of a strong and flexible model that captures many of the nuances of the thermodynamics of computation beyond logical reversibility. While current computational devices expend energy at rates well above those mandated by the laws of thermodynamics, as technology improves a principled understanding of thermodynamics is key to optimizing the energetic costs of computation.

However, most of the study of the thermodynamics of computation to date has been based on classical thermodynamics principles. While the field of thermodynamics itself has continued to evolve in recent decades, the study of the thermodynamics of computation has not kept pace. In particular, there has been a revolution in non-equilibrium statistical physics in the 21st century, resulting in what is now called _stochastic thermodynamics_. Whereas classical thermodynamics is, in its foundations, concerned only with systems at equilibrium, stochastic thermodynamics focuses on systems arbitrarily far from equilibrium. This makes it the ideal formalism for analyzing the thermodynamics of computation.

This paper serves two purposes: First, we introduce such a new model for investigating the thermodynamics of circuits. Our goal with this model is to strike a balance between broad accessibility to a general computer science audience and correctness with respect to stochastic thermodynamics, which represents our current best understanding of the fundamental energetic cost of machines, including computing machines. Second, we show how this circuit model can be leveraged to prove a wide range of new results ranging from the computational complexity of optimizing Boolean circuits to asymptotically tight lower and upper bounds on the thermodynamic costs of fixed circuits.

We start by giving a detailed overview of the history of the thermodynamics of computation before diving into our model and results.

## 1.1 Landauer’s principle and logical reversibility

Most of the computer science literature on the fundamental energetic costs of computation studies _reversible computing_,<sup>1</sup> This is an important and groundbreaking body of work, which we now summarize. Suppose a computing device executes a basic computational step that is _logically irreversible_, meaning that the device goes from logical state _c_<sub>0</sub> (such as the configuration of a multitape Turing machine, for instance) to logical state _c_<sub>1</sub>, where _c_<sub>1</sub> has _another_ predecessor state \(c'_0\) that also transitions to _c_<sub>1</sub> in one step. Formally, the global transition function \(\delta:C\rightarrow C\) mapping the machine’s current state to its next state is not injective. Landauer [Lan61] argued that this necessarily decreases entropy within the computing device, entropy must correspondingly increase<tbc>

<sup>1</sup>Notable exceptions abound in the physics literature, e.g., [WK20, YCW26, YYW26, Wol19a, WKL<sup>+</sup>24], but these papers generally use physics terms and assumptions that are often difficult for computer scientists to read.

<tbc>elsewhere in the universe to satisfy the Second Law of thermodynamics. Phrased in terms of _work_ (i.e., accessible energy), _Landauer’s principle_ states that _logically irreversible operations must expend work in order to release heat into their environments_.<sup>2</sup> Given a transition from _n_ equally likely predecessor states to _m_ equally likely successors, _k_Tln(_n/m_) heat must be released, regardless of the physical implementation of the operation. Here T denotes the system’s temperature<sup>3</sup> and _k_ is Boltzmann’s constant.<sup>4</sup>

Landauer argued \[Lan61\] that most real computation would necessarily execute many irreversible operations, implying an unavoidable cost of \(\Omega(tk\mathbb{T}ln2)\) to execute _t_ steps of a computation regardless of the physical implementation of the computing device. Bennett \[Ben73\] challenged this assumption, showing how to convert an arbitrary Turing machine _M_ into a logically reversible Turing machine _R_ computing the same function. The configuration graph of _R_ is then a 1D line \(c_0\rightarrow c_1\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow c_t\). A completely unbiased random walk on this graph, requiring no work to bias it forwards, would then visit final configuration _c<sub>t</sub>_ in _O(t_<sup>2</sup>) time on average.<sup>5</sup>

Bennett’s original construction \[Ben73\] simulates a _t_-step Turing machine in _O(t_) steps but pays with an increase in memory complexity up to \(\Theta(t)\), essentially needing to write down the entire history of the computation on a separate worktape to maintain logical reversibility, bringing the memory use up to asymptotically match the time. (Thus a polynomial-time, log-space computation, for example, pays exponentially extra memory to make the computation logically reversible.) A series of papers over the next few decades \[Ben89, LS90, LV96, LTV98, LMT00, BTV01\] showed various improved simulation time/space tradeoffs in reversible Turing machines; see \[Ben82, Vit05, Mor08\] for useful surveys. Toffoli and Fredkin \[Tof77, Tof80, FT82\] pioneered the study of reversible computation in other computational models such as cellular automata and circuits. Meanwhile in the physics community, there has been work on understanding the thermodynamics of logically reversible Turing machines \[SCSB15b, BJO21\].

So what is there to say about the fundamental thermodynamic costs of computation that has not already been said in the reversible computing literature? First, we may consider a situation in which we do not have access to a logically reversible gate set, in which we wish to understand the fundamental energetic costs associated with whatever computational devices we do have on hand. While there has been progress towards actually building logically reversible computational devices (e.g. \[AFK<sup>+</sup>98, Fra02, FBT<sup>+</sup>20\]), these systems are not yet ready for widespread use and most computation today is performed in a highly irreversible manner. This is a deep research issue<tbc>

<sup>2</sup>In this paper we use the term "release heat" mostly synonymously with "dissipate heat", but generally reserve the term "dissipate" to mean a loss of heat/work/useful energy that is irreversible. However, we are careful to include a descriptor such as "irreversible" or "irrecoverable" when we want to identify that the lose of heat/energy cannot be undone; absent this descriptor, any release/transfer of heat/work/useful energy in principle may be recovered. <sup>3</sup>In physics, it is common to specify a _heat bath_ of temperature T. For our purposes, we can think of T as the temperature of both the system and its environment. <sup>4</sup>Throughout this paper, we choose the units for measuring energy so that _k_Tln2=1. So we measure energy and heat in comparable units to bits. <sup>5</sup>Bennett \[Ben73\] observed that readout from such a device would be impractical, since even after waiting _t_<sup>2</sup> time, there is only a 1_/t_ probability of observing _R_ in its final output configuration. He proposed dissipating small \(\varepsilon\checkmark k\mathbb{T}ln2\) energy per step to bias the computation forward just enough to ensure a constant probability of finding the machine in an output configuration. This still implies \(\varepsilon t=\Omega(t)\) energy cost for a _t_-step computation. See \[DKL<sup>+</sup>24\] for arguments that this total cost need not scale linearly with _t_, essentially by using algorithmic design techniques to increase the probability of observing the machine in an output configuration even with totally unbiased transitions, obviating the need to supply energy for even a slight forward bias. However, this trick (and the original unbiased walk outlined in \[Ben73\]) doesn’t account for the thermodynamic costs of resetting the device (see \[Nor13, SCSB15a\]). In \[DKL<sup>+</sup>24\] the authors avoid these costs by designing a device that never needs to be reset.

<tbc>in its own right, and more practically, reflects the situation in almost every deployed computational system.

Second, over the last few decades the field of non-equilibrium statistical physics has undergone major developments, culminating in a new subfield called _stochastic thermodynamics_ [VdBE15, Sei25]. These developments have upended our understanding of the thermodynamics of physical systems that implement computation. In particular, they reveal that the traditional understanding of logical reversibility and Landauer’s principle is at best partially correct: while the Second Law does indeed imply that decreasing entropy of a system locally requires increasing entropy outside the system, nothing in the Second Law says that this must be a physically irreversible loss of work.

To give a simple example of a logically irreversible process that can be done in a physically/thermodynamically reversible way (i.e., can be done with arbitrarily little dissipated work), suppose we have a particle in a cylinder, and identify the particle being in the top half of the cylinder as a bit 1, while the particle being in the bottom half is identified as bit 0, with equal probability. So if we compress the cylinder to its bottom half using a piston, we perform a bit erasure, since afterwards the particle is guaranteed to be in the bottom half. Moreover, in first-year physics we learn that if this compression is done sufficiently slowly, then all the work expended in that compression can be recovered afterward simply by _uncompressing_ the cylinder sufficiently slowly, returning it to its original volume, and returning the particle’s distribution to equally likely to be in either half (see Szilard engines for more details, [Szi29, KMPA14]).

This is precisely the property that defines a process as being thermodynamically reversible. In contrast, if one compresses the cylinder too quickly, no matter how one subsequently uncompresses the cylinder, one won’t recover all the work that was used in the compression. This is what is meant by thermodynamic irreversibility. This example illustrates that logical and thermodynamic reversibility are independent properties of a process; it is possible to have one without the other. (See [Sag14] for a pedagogical elaboration of this point.)

Third, if the function _f_ being computed is not injective, it is not possible to compute the mapping \(x\mapsto f(x)\) in a logically reversibly way; instead reversible computing models typically compute \(x\mapsto(x,f(x))\). But the mappings \(x\rightarrow f(x)\) and \(x\rightarrow(x,f(x))\) are fundamentally different. If _f_ is non-injective or if _f_<sup>-1</sup> is prohibitively expensive to compute (i.e., if _f_ is a one-way function), then it is impossible to efficiently and reversibly obtain just _f(x_) from the pair (_x,f(x_)).<sup>6</sup> One might think it is okay to just leave an extra copy of _x_ in your computer’s memory, but if you compute _f_ repeatedly and old values of _x_ are overwritten, the cost of erasing these old values must be paid (see [Wol19a, Sec.11]). One might hope to store values of _x_ generated by intermediate steps of a larger logically reversible computation and reversibly uncompute them during the uncomputation step, however, temporarily storing _x_ increases the space complexity of the overall computation (see [Ben89]).

Finally, it remains open whether every time-_t_, space-_s_ Turing machine can be simulated by a<tbc>

<sup>6</sup>Bennett [Ben73] shows that, if _f_ is injective, it is possible to compute the mapping \(x\mapsto f(x)\) reversibly (i.e., not needing the input also to appear as part of the output). However, this construction has time complexity as high as the max of computing _f and_ computing _f_<sup>-1</sup>, since it involves taking a direct computation of _f_<sup>-1</sup> by a Turing machine and making it logically reversible in the same way that _f_ is reversibly computed. But if we want the time complexity to be no worse than that of computing _f_, this rules out one-way functions in which _f_<sup>-1</sup> has time complexity fundamentally greater than that of _f_. Indeed, it is well-known folklore that the mapping \(x\mapsto f(x)\) cannot be efficiently computed in a logically reversible manner if _f_ is a one-way function: if such a computation, for example a Boolean circuit, were completely logically reversible, starting only with _x_ and ending only with _f(x_), then the mirror image of such a circuit would be an equally efficient circuit computing _f_<sup>-1</sup>, contradicting that _f_ is one-way.

In this paper we start to investigate how stochastic thermodynamics can help untangle these issues.

## 1.2 Beyond logical reversibility: Stochastic thermodynamics

Bennett’s approach of requiring logical reversibility of every computational step is in one sense a very ambitious way to minimize energy costs by pushing the so-called _Landauer cost_ of executing logically irreversible operations to 0, simply by removing all such operations. Li and Vitányi \[LV96\] investigated how it is possible to trade time and space for ‘energy’ by limiting the number of logically irreversible steps in a computation. Demaine, Lynch, Mirano, and Tyagi \[DLMT16\] built on this idea and proposed a generalization of logical reversibility they call _semi-reversible computing_, in which irreversible operations \(f:D\rightarrow R\) are permitted and assumed to cost log \(\frac{|D|}{|R|}\) bits of energy to execute (this being the natural generalization of the Landauer cost of 1 bit when |_D_|=2 and |_R_|=1, assuming a uniform distribution on _D_). The total energy cost (by this definition) is then treated as a complexity measure to be minimized.

However, the more modern field of _stochastic thermodynamics_ \[VdBE15, Sei25\] has generalized our understanding of the interaction of entropy and fundamental energy use in physical devices, beyond the overly simplistic assumption that each bit erasure costs _k_Tln2 energy. It has been argued \[WKL<sup>+</sup>24\] that stochastic thermodynamics can be fruitfully applied to computational complexity to better understand the relationship between fundamental thermodynamic costs and other traditional complexity measures such as time and space.

We now review _entropy production_, a basic concept from modern stochastic thermodynamics that lets us study the fundamental limits of energetic costs even for logically irreversible computation. As applied to the study of computation, we propose entropy production as a computational complexity measure/cost to be minimized. This is already the measure of interest for such systems in the physics community (i.e. \[Wol19a, PP21, WKL<sup>+</sup>24, Sei25\]). We then analyze these costs in a particular circuit model, noting that our approach can be extended in a natural way to other models of computation.

We provide our full definitions in Section 2 and give a semi-formal summary of the underlying concepts here. Briefly, the generalization of the Second Law of thermodynamics most central to our purpose is the equation

\(\mathsf{EP}=\mathsf{Q}-(\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_0)-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_1)).\) (1)

Equation (1) appears later in Definition 2.24 with notation specialized to the study of the thermodynamics of circuits. The terms EP and Q respectively mean _entropy production_ and _entropy flow_. However, throughout this paper we focus on the case of a single (thermal) reservoir. That leads us to use the term _heat released_ for Q. Furthermore, given our choice of units such that _k_Tln2=1, we can equate information in bits with equal units of heat; we discuss these terms below.

To begin, we focus on the term S(D<sub>0</sub>)-S(D<sub>1</sub>) in Eq. (1). D<sub>0</sub> represents the probability distribution on states of a physical device<sup>7</sup> prior to executing a (possibly logically irreversible) step,<tbc>

<sup>7</sup>The stochastic thermodynamic perspective can be viewed as an "intrinsically distributional" complexity measure because it defines costs that are fundamentally tied to a distribution over inputs. In other words, there is not in general a sensible notion of "worst-case entropy production" defined as \(max_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\mathsf{EP}(x)\), as is typical for definitions

and D<sub>1</sub> represents the associated distribution after; \(\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D})=\sum_{x\in\mathrm{supp}(\mathcal{D})}\mathrm{Pr}[x]\mathrm{log}\frac{1}{\mathrm{Pr}[x]}\) is the _Shannon entropy_ of D.<sup>8</sup>

Concretely, suppose we perform the most widely discussed logical operation in the thermodynamics of computing: erasing a single bit \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Here "erasing _b_" generally means "setting _b_ to 0", i.e., no matter whether _b_ was 0 or 1 before, afterward it is 0 and so the system has "erased" any knowledge of _b_’s previous value. In this case, D<sub>1</sub> is the degenerate point-mass distribution with Pr<sub>D<sub>1</sub></sub>\[_b_=0\]=1. The prior distribution D<sub>0</sub> may be a number of things, but the worst case in terms of logical irreversibility is the uniform distribution D with Pr<sub>D<sub>0</sub></sub>\[_b_=0\]=Pr<sub>D<sub>0</sub></sub>\[_b_=1\]=1/2, i.e., prior to erasing the bit, we have maximal uncertainty about its current value. The term S(D<sub>0</sub>)-S(D<sub>1</sub>), the difference in Shannon entropy between distributions D<sub>0</sub> and D<sub>1</sub>, is the so-called _Landauer cost_.<sup>9</sup> In this example, _S_ is the simple binary entropy function on _p_=Pr<sub>D<sub>_i_</sub></sub>\[_b_=0\], so S(D<sub>0</sub>)=1, S(D<sub>1</sub>)=0, and the Landauer cost is 1 bit of entropy. Importantly, (1) means that the Landauer cost does not necessarily imply positive entropy production. By focusing instead on entropy production, we open the door to modeling and analyzing sources of heat dissipation in computation, over and above the Landauer cost, that cause EP to be positive.

The other two terms EP and Q account for how this local drop in entropy relates to the outside universe. EP, the _entropy production_, represents the total increase in entropy of the universe. The Second Law dictates that \(\mathsf{EP}\ge 0\). This is related to the _local_ decrease in entropy S(D<sub>0</sub>)-S(D<sub>1</sub>) by the _heat released_ Q.<sup>10</sup> Q corresponds to the entropy change of the environment due to heat exchange (releasing heat increases the entropy of the environment) and encompasses the underlying physical implementation of our computation. Note that to maintain the Second Law (\(\mathsf{EP}\ge 0\)), we must have \(\mathsf{Q}\ge\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_0)-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_1)\). If the local entropy strictly dropped through a logically irreversible step, i.e., if S(D<sub>0</sub>)_\>_S(D<sub>1</sub>), then in this case Q must be strictly positive to maintain \(\mathsf{EP}\ge 0\).

The ability of randomized computation to have a negative Landauer cost has implications for energy use as well, allowing a computation to use randomized operations to counteract the heat released in other steps by logically irreversible operations. As a simple example of these principles in action, and to illustrate how the laws of physics allow for computation with zero dissipated work _even if_ a logically irreversible step such as erasing a bit is performed, consider a situation in which we first generate a random bit and then erase it. Imagine we have some physical sort of randomness/entropy available to generate a random bit \(b\in\{0,1\}\). Suppose we generate this bit in<tbc>

Applying equation (1) to the first step, we have that D<sub>0</sub> is the point-mass Pr<sub>D<sub>0</sub></sub>\[_b_=0\]=1, whereas afterward we have Pr<sub>D<sub>1</sub></sub>\[_b_=0\]=Pr<sub>D<sub>1</sub></sub>\[_b_=1\]=1/2. Thus the Landauer cost S(D<sub>0</sub>)-S(D<sub>1</sub>)=-1 is actually _negative_. Physically, this corresponds to the fact that in principle, one removes _k_Tln2 heat from the environment to randomize this bit, releasing the same amount of heat on the subsequent erasure step that takes us from D<sub>1</sub> (_b_ is equally likely to be 0 or 1) back to D<sub>0</sub> (_b_=0). This is essentially "taking a loan and then paying it back".

In the remainder of this paper, we focus on deterministic computation, in which every state has at most one successor. Our model may describe only part of a larger physical device: other parts may perform randomized operations with negative Landauer cost and draw heat from the environment to offset heat released by the deterministic computation. When \(f:D\rightarrow R\) is a (deterministic, single-valued) function being computed, we let L_<sub>f</sub>_(D) (Definition 2.19) denote S(D)-S(_f_(D)), where _f_(D) denotes the distribution on _R_ induced by distribution D on _D_. In this case, the data processing inequality (Definition 2.5) implies that \(\mathcal{L}_f(\mathcal{D})\ge 0\); i.e., a deterministic process cannot increase the entropy of a distribution.

The previous example shows that a logically irreversible operation may have zero entropy production. Next we discuss a "dual" example: an overall operation can be logically reversible, yet require positive entropy production due to "locality", i.e., due to the fact that portions of the computation must be done in physically separate places, so that despite entropy staying constant globally, local operations must produce entropy due to lack of knowledge of rest of the state of the system. Consider three entities Alice, Bob, and Eve. Alice and Bob are at physically separate locations with no ability to communicate. Eve has a uniformly random bit _b_, and sends a copy of _b_ to each of Alice and Bob. Alice must erase her bit, setting it to 0. Globally, this is logically reversible, since the mapping \((b,b)\mapsto(0,b)\) is injective, but since Alice "locally forgets" _b_, she must release a unit of heat into the environment to erase her bit, even though far-away Bob remembers _b_. Though this example may seem contrived and hand-wavey, it is in fact a good example of what we sometimes called _modularity cost_ (also known as _modularity mismatch cost_ in the stochastic thermodynamics literature, e.g., \[Wol19b\]): the fact that a self-contained computational module, such as a gate in a circuit, must release heat to compute an irreversible _local_ operation, despite the fact that elsewhere in the circuit, information about the gate’s input is retained and so globally, the operation is reversible.

To summarize, (1) applied to deterministic computation of a function _f_ obeys EP=Q-L_<sub>f</sub>_(D). L_<sub>f</sub>_(D) is a purely information theoretic term depending only on _f_ and the input distribution D: the loss of entropy S(D)-S(_f_(D)) between the input distribution D to _f_ and the induced output distribution _f_(D). Reversible computing literature is concerned with making L_<sub>f</sub>_(D)=0 for every computational step; in this paper we allow it to be positive, though we freely and regularly use reversible computing techniques as well. Q is the heat released into the environment during this computation; this depends on the physics of the device computing _f_. The Second Law of Thermodynamics states that \(\mathsf{EP}\ge 0\), so since EP=Q-L_<sub>f</sub>_(D), this implies \(\mathsf{Q}\ge\mathcal{L}_f(\mathcal{D})\). From a complexity-theoretic perspective, we wish to minimize EP, since it represents a physically irreversible loss of work (useful energy). However, given a fixed _f_ to compute and distribution D, we have no control over L_<sub>f</sub>_(D), so minimizing Q is equivalent to minimizing EP.

## 1.3 Prior work on thermodynamics of circuits

One perspective on the thermodynamic costs of circuits is provided by works of Michael Frank [Fra17, Fra18]. In [Fra17], Frank generalizes the conventional computer science notion of logical reversibility to include operations that, while not reversible in general, are so under a restricted subset of their inputs. He denotes such operations as being "conditionally reversible" and shows that they can be implemented to release arbitrarily little heat, so long as the gates never receive an input violating the reversibility precondition. Frank is primarily interested in conditional reversibility since it gives logically reversible gates that may be easier to implement than networks of Toffoli gates. Our work can be seen as a further generalization of this idea; in addition to allowing conditionally reversible gates to release zero expected heat on valid distributions over inputs, we consider gates that are finely tuned for the actual distribution over inputs they expect to receive. In [Fra18], Frank also points out that Q is not quite the correct measure of thermodynamic cost. He points out that the thermodynamic costs associated with Landauer’s principle is not merely the fact that Q must be positive. Rather it is that information which is dissipated as heat will rapidly become unrecoverable to the computational process, resulting in something similar to what we call a modularity cost. Frank justifies the study of logically reversible computing since it is a sufficient condition to avoid Landauer related thermodynamic costs.

Prior work by Wolpert, Kolchinsky, Caravelli, Yadav, and Yousef [WK20, YCW26, YYW26] investigated the thermodynamics of Boolean circuits using the theorems involving _mismatch cost_ -- a metric that quantifies the additional entropy production incurred by running a process on a different input distribution than the "ideal" one for given hardware. In this case, the physics of the device computing the gate may, in a sense, be "summarized information-theoretically" by an _optimal_ input distribution D<sup>∗</sup>, the distribution that minimizes the entropy production according to (1). They show lower bounds on the entropy production induced by running a circuit on a (potentially mismatched) input distribution D, where the lower bound depends only on the logical behavior of the gates with respect to an optimal input distribution D<sup>∗</sup>. In other words, it is possible to prove non-trivial lower bounds on the EP of a circuit without knowing any details of the physical implementation of its gates other than their optimal distributions over its inputs.<sup>11</sup>

The perspective of these works is that we know an optimal input distribution for a gate, and proceeds from there to measure mismatch costs (which are a lower bound on EP). Mismatch costs are a powerful tool for analyzing thermodynamic costs without needing to specify the underlying physics, but they are cumbersome to work with. The thermodynamic accounting they provide requires viewing everything through the lens of distributions over state and costs are neither linear (with respect to the probabilities of inputs) nor local to the gates performing computation. Moreover, the optimal distribution for a gate is a counter-intuitive way to specify its behavior and such a distribution is not unique even when the dynamics of the gate are deterministic.<sup>12</sup>

Nevertheless, these methods are particularly nice as with mild assumptions on the behavior of gates in a circuit (i.e. modularity or time-invariant behavior), they can prove entropy lower bounds that are truly independent of the underlying hardware.

<sup>11</sup>The physical implementation does influence what is the optimal distribution. The significance of mismatch cost is that it can be measured knowing _only_ what is the optimal distribution, i.e., the physical implementation influences the mismatch cost _only_ through how it influences what is the optimal distribution. <sup>12</sup>There is a well defined way to handle this with mismatch costs, but it requires analyzing the pre-image of each possible output independently, but this can be messy to work with.

## 1.4 Our results

Here we provide a high level overview of our results and the techniques we use to obtain them.

### The thermodynamic circuit model

We introduce a model of circuits where each gate releases heat determined by its input value in order to perform logically irreversible computation. For a circuit to compute a function _f_, we require it to map each input state \((x,\vec{0})\) to output state \((f(x),\vec{0})\); the \(\vec{0}\)’s (which have different lengths if \(|x|\neq|f(x)|\)) denote "ancilla" wires that may be used as extra storage during the computation. In other words, the circuit must erase any "dirty" bits introduced during the computation including the original value of _x_. The amount of heat a gate releases can depend on that gate’s input; imagine that the gate must undergo some physical process to map each of its possible input states to the correct output. Thus, we can assign a "heat function" to each gate \(Q:\{0,1\}^n\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{\infty\}\) that maps each input to an associated amount of released heat. Technically, the amount of heat released by this process may not be deterministic, so one should think of these values as being expected costs, though sometimes for brevity we may say a gate releases _Q(x_) heat on input _x_, understood to mean _expected_ heat. Thanks to the linearity of expectation, this does not make a difference in the details of our model. We say a heat function for a gate is _valid_ if it obeys the Second Law of thermodynamics (i.e. the EP in (1) is always non-negative) on every marginal input distribution. From this perspective, we connect our model to mismatch costs in Appendix C of the appendix, and show that some of the results in \[WK20, YCW26, YYW26\] have more intuitive proofs using heat functions. We also show how our model can be used to prove new results about the thermodynamic costs of circuits.

Recall from Section 1.2 that our goal is to minimize EP, and that once L_<sub>f</sub>_(D) is fixed, minimizing EP is equivalent to minimizing Q. Despite this equivalence once L_<sub>f</sub>_(D) is fixed, when we prove a one-way bound, we generally prove lower bounds on EP (i.e., negative results stating that some computation _must_ dissipate a certain minimum amount of work that cannot be recovered) and upper bounds on Q (i.e., positive results stating that it is _possible_ to achieve a certain computation while only releasing a small amount of heat). For deterministic computation, \(\mathsf{EP}\le\mathsf{Q}\) so a lower bound on EP is also a lower bound on Q and an upper bound on Q is also an upper bound on EP. As is typical in theoretical computer science, we will use _O_-notation to suppress constant factors in our bounds. Note that constant factors are important to track in the case where \(\mathsf{Q}=\Omega(h(n))\) and L_<sub>f</sub>_(D)=_O(h(n_)). Depending on the hidden constants, the EP for such a computation could be anywhere between 0 and \(\Omega(h(n))\).

There are two important caveats with our approach in this paper. First, when discussing EP, we are implicitly assuming that the input distribution to our circuit is sampled independently from any larger context. If a copy of the input to a circuit is retained somewhere outside of the circuit, then the drop in entropy in (1) should actually be zero and we get that EP=Q. When proving lower bounds on EP this is a non-issue, as the additional context can only increase the EP. When proving upper bounds on EP, we specify that we are interested in the _circuit entropy production_, which we define as EP under this assumption on the input distribution. Second, when giving upper bounds on either the Q or the EP of a circuit, we are operating under the "axiom" that every gate could in principle be built with any valid heat function. While the validity constraint protects our gates from violating the Second Law of thermodynamics, other physical or engineering constraints may theoretically prevent such a gate from existing. For example, speed limit theorems \[SFS18\] imply that, with bounds on transition rates, EP must be strictly positive in order for gates to<tbc>

compute their outputs in finite time<sup>13</sup> and current CMOS technology is far from the thermodynamic limit imposed by validity. Thus our upper bounds should be interpreted under the "spherical cow" assumption that validity is the only constraint on realizable heat functions.

## Hardness results and approximation algorithms for computing optimal heat functions

Section 4 is concerned with computing the optimal heat functions for gates in a given Boolean circuit (so as to minimize EP), assuming the i.i.d. uniform distribution for the circuit’s inputs. We first show that the problem of computing the optimal heat function for each gate (so as to minimize total entropy production of the entire circuit) is unfortunately PP-complete (Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4). Since Lemma 3.1 shows how to compute the optimal heat function for a _single_ gate and a given input distribution to that gate, this hardness follows essentially from the fact that computing the induced input distribution for a given gate in a circuit, knowing that the circuit’s inputs are i.i.d. with probability 1/2, is itself PP-complete. The (straightforward) reduction is from the PP-complete language L<sub>SAT/2</sub> of Boolean circuits C where at least half the assignments satisfy C: by adding a single erasure gate _g_ on the output, with an optimal heat function _Q<sub>g</sub>_, \(Q_g(1)\le 1\) if and only if \(Pr[\text{output of}\mathcal{C}\text{is}1]\ge 1/2\), i.e., if and only if \(\mathcal{C}\in\mathcal{L}_{\text{SAT}/2}\). Containment in PP directly follows from an algorithm that accepts or rejects depending on the relative probabilities a gate receives a specified input _x_ or another input \(x'\neq x\) where \(f(x')=f(x)\).

Since PP-hardness rules out polynomial-time exact algorithms, this motivates the question of whether polynomial-time approximation algorithms exist. We show that this depends crucially on the form of error. With _multiplicative_ error, i.e., for some constant _c\>_1, to compute heat functions with expected value at most _c times_ optimal, then this is NP-hard, i.e., untractable unless \(\text{NP}\subseteq\text{BPP}\). There is an easy argument for this: suppose we have a Boolean formula \(\phi\) (a special type of circuit) and want to know whether \(\phi\) is satisfiable. If we then add an erasure gate _g_ to \(\phi\)’s output, then for an optimal heat function \(Q_g^*\), if \(\phi\) is unsatisfiable, \(Q_g^*(0)=0\), i.e., it costs 0 heat to erase the output since we know it is 0. If \(\phi\) is satisfiable, then \(Q_g^*(0)>0\). Thus any approximation algorithm outputting heat value _q_ will tell us whether \(\phi\) is satisfiable depending on whether _q\>_0. However, this is a somewhat degenerate case, in the sense that _any_ optimization problem permitting an optimal value of 0 has the property that no multiplicative approximation is good unless it is exact. The more interesting case is when a wire might have both bits 0 or 1 (supp(D)={0,1}), so that we have a positive optimal expected heat E<sub>_x_∼D</sub>\[_Q_<sup>∗</sup>(_x_)\]_\>_0. We can in fact prove NP-hardness of multiplicative approximation continues to hold even in this case (Lemma 4.7).

## Bounds on thermodynamic costs of fixed circuits

Having shown the difficulty in computing optimal heat functions for arbitrary given circuits, Section 5 then analyzes particular circuits and derives both lower bounds on EP and upper bounds on Q. Section 5.1 begins with a warm-up exercise analyzing the computation of the _n_-input AND function \(x_1\wedge x_2\wedge\dots\wedge x_n\) on uniformly distributed inputs in {0,1}_<sup>n</sup>_, using only input-preserving binary-AND gates of the form \(\wedge(x_1,x_2,z)=(x_1,x_2,x_1\wedge x_2)\) and erasure gates _E(x_)=0. We show the (possibly) counterintuitive result that the most natural implementation, a tree of AND gates of depth _O_(log_n_), along with appropriate erasure gates to enable the circuit to cleanly compute the 1-bit output \(x_1\wedge x_2\wedge\dots\wedge x_n\), has circuit entropy production \(\Omega(n)\), whereas the "serial" variant with depth \(\Theta(n)\), can be done with circuit entropy production that is only _O_(1).

Section 5.2 then analyzes the _O(n_log<sup>2</sup>_n_)-gate, _O_(log<sup>2</sup>_n_)-depth Batcher even-odd mergesort sorting network on Boolean inputs. When applied to Boolean values, sorting networks are circuits where every gate is a 2-input, 2-output _comparator_ gate: computing the identity on inputs 00,01,11, but on input 10, swapping the bits to output 01. The main results of this section, Theorems 5.2 and 5.4, show an _O(n_) upper bound on Q using only _O_(log_n_) distinct heat functions and a matching \(\Omega(n)\) lower bound on EP over a uniform distribution of inputs in {0,1}_<sup>n</sup>_ when using the optimal valid heat function on every gate. ## Compaction and sorting with zero entropy production

Section 6.1 shows that we can do better than Batcher by designing a bit-sorting (a.k.a., _bit-compaction_) circuit specifically to minimize EP, and in fact can achieve zero circuit entropy production (Theorem 6.1) on any exchangeable distribution over inputs. Note that this construction is not a sorting network, as it uses ancilla wires and more general gates than only comparators.

We do so by using standard Bennett-style "compute/copy output/uncompute" (applied to circuits) to convert any circuit computing the mapping \(x\mapsto f(x)\) to one reversibly computing \((x,\vec{0})\mapsto(x,f(x))\),<sup>16</sup> with only a constant increase in gate and depth complexity.<sup>17</sup> Once we have (_x,f(x_)) in memory, we give a way to pick heat functions for erasing each bit of _x_ such that the expected heat released is exactly the drop in entropy from mapping _x_ to _f(x_). The choice of heat function for erasing each _x<sub>i</sub>_ is determined based on the value of _f(x_) and the suffix of _x_ after index _i_, which can be computed and uncomputed in a logically reversible fashion even after _x<sub>i</sub>_ has been erased. We design such a circuit based on any sorting network _C_ with _t(n_) gates and depth _d(n_) that compacts _n_ inputs with _m_ bit payloads using only constant arity gates with only _O(t(n)m+n_<sup>2</sup>) gates, _O(d(n_)log_m+n_log_n_) depth, and _O(t(n_)+_nm_) ancilla wires. In Section 6.2, we show how this approach can be extended to give zero circuit entropy production circuits for sorting on any exchangeable distribution over inputs.

## New proofs of known results on mismatch cost and circuit mutual information using heat functions

Following some basic lemmas in Appendix A of the appendix and the aforementioned analysis of Batcher’s sorting algorithm in Appendix B, we prove new results connecting heat functions to mismatch costs and reprove existing results on mismatch costs using the language of heat functions in Appendices C and D. This is intended to share these insights from stochastic thermodynamics with the computer science community and better connect our heat function model with prior work on the thermodynamics of circuits. Appendix C concerns _mismatch cost_, which is informally defined as the _extra_ entropy production incurred by using a gate with a heat function optimal for distribution D<sup>∗</sup>, when in fact \(\mathcal{D}\neq\mathcal{D}^*\) is the true distribution. The mismatch cost of course depends on the physical implementation of the gate. Throughout this paper we analyze how much entropy a computational device must release into its environment to obey the second law of thermodynamics. We will be assuming that each logical state of the machine has the same energy level and number of microstates.18 In principle this entropy can take many forms, but for our analysis it is safe to assume that it is always released as heat. This motivates what we will call _heat functions_ as a way to abstract away messy details for how computations release excess entropy. 18We use the term "microstate" in this paper to mean the various different physical states a machine can be in while still representing the same logical state. As a concrete example, a Boolean gate implemented with semiconductors has a logical state identified by the bits on the input and output wires, which generally will correspond to many different physical microstates, depending on the precise positions and motion of electrons in the wires.

## Thermodynamic circuits

We start by giving two working definitions of circuits that we use in this paper. We start with our model of circuits, which is heavily inspired by ‘serial reinitialized’ model introduced in \[WK20\].

This model of circuits should be familiar to readers acquainted with the quantum circuit model. For those unfamiliar with such models, recall that a standard model defines a Boolean circuit as a directed acyclic graph, where each edge represents a wire connecting exactly two gates (nodes). Instead, in our model, all information is stored in a fixed set of _n_ wires, and gates operate on a subset (typically of _O_(1)-size) of these wires to update their values. However, unlike quantum circuits, we do not require gates to be unitary. Instead, they can perform any arbitrary mapping on their associated wires. While we use the language of circuits with wires and gates, this formulation works equally well to describe straight line programs where wires correspond to registers and gates correspond to operations on these registers. While we define such circuits in abstract, as is common in complexity theory, it will often be interesting to restrict them to specific gate sets (thus each gate would operate on _O_(1) wires independently of the total number of wires). This rules out the possibility of implementing arbitrary functions with a single gate acting simultaneously on all wires of the circuit and lets us analyze the thermodynamic costs of computations with restricted gate sets.<sup>19</sup>

**Definition 2.15.** _A deterministic_ circuit C _on n inputs with T gates and_ \(W\ge n\) _wires is described as an ordered collection of T gates g<sub>t</sub>_=(_I<sub>g<sub>t</sub></sub>,f<sup>g<sub>t</sub></sup>_) _for_ \(t\in\{1,\dots,T\}\)_. Each gate specifies a set_ \(I_{g_t}\subseteq[W]\) _and a function_ \(f^{g_t}:\Sigma^{I_{g_t}}\rightarrow\Sigma^{I_{g_t}}\)_. On input_ \(x_1,\dots x_n\in\Sigma^n\) _the circuit starts in the state_ \(\mathcal{C}^0\in\Sigma^W\) _where_ \(\mathcal{C}_i^0=x_i\) _for_ \(i\in[n]\) _and_ \(\mathcal{C}_i^0=0\) _for_ \(i\in[W]\backslash[n]\)_. The_ state _of the circuit at step t is given by_ \(\mathcal{C}^t=f_\uparrow^{g_t}(\mathcal{C}^{t-1})\)_. We say that wire_ \(i\in[W]\) _of_ C evaluates to \(x\in\Sigma\) _when_ \(\mathcal{C}_i^T=x\).

Note that Definition 2.15 allows to have more wires (_W_) than input bits (_n_), to allow extra "workspace" for computation. It requires all non-input wires to be initially 0. The next definition captures our notion of computing output, which similarly allows the number of output bits _m_ to be strictly less than the number of wires _W_, and similarly requires that at the end of the computation, all non-output wires are 0.<sup>20</sup>

**Definition 2.16.** _We say that a circuit_ C cleanly computes _a function_ \(f:\Sigma^n\rightarrow\Sigma^m\) _if on every input_ \(x\in\Sigma^n\)_, wire i of_ C _evaluates to f<sub>i</sub>(x_) _if_ \(i\le m\) _and evaluates to_ 0 _if i\>m._<sup>21</sup>

<sup>19</sup> As with the standard DAG-based model of Boolean circuits, if one allows larger gates than _O_(1), even up to a single gate taking all inputs and computing an arbitrary Boolean function in one step, then this will not give informative complexity measures. In this paper, restricting gates to operate on _O_(1) wires will enable stronger lower bounds on entropy production, in an analogous sense that restricting standard Boolean circuits to have _O_(1)-size gates enables nontrivial lower bounds on gate complexity. <sup>20</sup>This requirement of zeroing out non-output wires is particularly important in the context of thermodynamics of computing, because it forces on the circuit the obligation to erase any non-output bits left over from the computation. Absent this requirement, a circuit could appear naïvely to produce less entropy than one would expect, hiding the cost of erasing those leftover "garbage" bits. However, if one wished to reuse the circuit for a subsequent computation, since those bits would at some point need to be set to 0 to prepare the circuit for the next input. The definition of clean computation forces the circuit to prepare itself for reuse. (Note that we do _not_ account for the thermodynamic cost of writing the input, recording the output, or replacing the old output with the new input.) <sup>21</sup>The choice to make the _first m_ wires correspond to output is arbitrary. If a circuit places its output on other wires, logically reversible swap gates can move the output to the first _m_ wires with no extra entropy production.

**Definition 2.17.** _A_ thermodynamic circuit _is a circuit_ C _where each gate g computing a function with domain D is assigned a_ heat function \(Q_g:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{\infty\}\)_. On input_ \(x\in D\)_, the gate releases Q<sub>g</sub>(x_) _expected heat into the environment._

**Remark 2.18.** _As we are fixing the temperature, it is reasonable to view Q as expected heat release. A more generally accurate description of Q(x_) _would be the expected entropy flow out of the system on input x._

As we will see in Appendix D, it is important to note that _Q_ is only allowed to depend on the inputs to a gate. This represents the fact that a gate is modular and oblivious to the larger state of the circuit. Otherwise, these heat functions can in principle be an arbitrary function of _D_. A gate that releases \(\infty\) heat on some input _x_ can be thought of being designed so it is not physically possible to specify _x_. This conveys the notion of restricted reversibility in \[Fra17\], where Frank points out that some logically irreversible operations can become reversible with such restrictions on their domain. However, not all choices of heat functions are valid. The Second Law of Thermodynamics (or Landauer’s costs) places constraints on the possible heat functions that can be assigned to each gate.

**Definition 2.19** (Landauer cost, \[Lan61\])**.** _For any function_ \(f:D\rightarrow R\) _and distribution_ D _over D, we define the_ Landauer cost _function of f on_ D:

\(\mathcal{L}_f(\mathcal{D})=\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D})-\mathcal{S}(f(\mathcal{D})).\)

The following is a corollary of the Second Law of Thermodynamics as applied to computation of functions. As a physical law, it cannot be proven in full generality, though it can be proven within specific models. We state it formally to motivate the subsequent Definition 2.21.

**Proposition 2.20** (Second law, \[Lan61, Sei05\])**.** _Let_ \(f:D\rightarrow R\) _be a function. Any physical process that maps every state_ \(x\in D\) _to the state f(x_) _must release at least_ L_<sub>f</sub>_(D) _expected heat when x is sampled from distribution_ D _over D._

In the context of physical systems evolving according to _f_, this is simply the lower bound on the expected heat release (or more generally entropy flow) out of a system where all logical configurations contain the same number of microstates as given by the second law of thermodynamics. The following definition essentially formalizes our notion of a heat function being compatible with the second law.

**Definition 2.21.** _Let g be a gate in circuit computing a function f with domain D. A heat function_ \(Q:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{\infty\}\) _is_ valid _for g if and only if, for every input distribution_ D _over D, we have that:_

\(\mathcal{L}_f(\mathcal{D})\le\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[Q(x)].\)

Definition 2.21 "directly" captures what we mean by a valid heat function--no matter the distribution it obeys the Second Law--and as stated intuitively appears to require validation over all input distributions over _D_. The following equivalent formulation of Definition 2.21 shows that validity in fact is solely a property of the value _Q(x_) on _individual_ inputs _x_. This is the deterministic specialization of Turgut’s Theorem 1 (Eq. (1)) in the simplified setting where each logical state has the same internal entropy \[Tur09\]. Zhu \[Zhu24\] subsequently rederived the same stochastic realizability criterion from a differential fluctuation theorem; with deterministic dynamics, Zhu’s condition likewise reduces to Lemma 2.22. We give a self-contained proof of Lemma 2.22 in Appendix A.

**Lemma 2.22.** _Let g be a gate in a circuit computing a function_ \(f:D\rightarrow R\)_. A heat function_ \(Q:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{\infty\}\) _is valid for g if and only if, for every_ \(y\in R\),

\(\sum_{x\in f^{-1}(y)}2^{-Q(x)}\le 1.\)

In practice, there is a large gap between valid heat functions (those obeying the Second Law) and physically realizable heat functions (which may release far _more_ heat than the minimum dictated by the Second Law, e.g., current CMOS technology). Additional heat is released by computation to drive the physical processes that implement the logical mapping of the gate in the desired direction in finite time \[SFS18\]. However, valid heat functions let us prove lower bounds on the thermodynamic costs of a computation and provide a limit for the physical implementation of the computation. In this paper, we state upper bounds on thermodynamic costs that make the idealized assumption that any combination of logical gate _g_ and valid heat function _Q_ for _g_ could actually be constructed. The known laws of physics neither explicitly construct such gates nor rule out their existence (in the quasistatic limit). Thus our upper bounds all implicitly require the following "spherical cow" like assumption.

**Assumption 2.23** (Idealized realizability assumption)**.** _Let_ \(f:D\rightarrow R\) _be any function and_ \(Q:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{\infty\}\) _be any valid heat function for computing f. Then we assume that it is possible to fabricate a gate that computes f while releasing Q(x_) _expected heat on each input where_ \(Q(x)\neq\infty\) _in the quasistatic (i.e. infinitely slowly) limit. We assume that whenever_ \(Q(x)=\infty\) _the gate is implemented in a way where it physically cannot receive such an input. In other words, the gate actually computes a restriction of f on inputs where Q(x_) _is finite._<sup>22</sup><tbc>

<sup>22</sup>The fact that \(Q(x)=\infty\) already makes this domain restriction implicit in our model. Any distribution with support on such an input would immediately make Q infinite. Thus heat functions where \(Q(x)=\infty\) on any input occurring with positive probability trivially satisfy lower bounds and would automatically make any resulting upper bound trivial.

This is well motivated. Theorem 2 of Turgut \[Tur09\] shows how, in an idealized model, it is possible to implement any fixed mapping from _D_ to _R_ where the expected released heat on every input exactly matches any valid _Q_. If one wishes to reject this assumption, then they should interpret all of our upper bounds on Q and EP as theoretical limits on the best possible lower bounds for these quantities that could be proven in our model. All of our lower bounds on EP and Q hold independently of this axiom.

Excess heat released by a physical process is called the entropy production \[Sei12\]. More formally (recall Definition 2.2 of \(f_\uparrow\)),

**Definition 2.24** (gate entropy production)**.** _Let_ C _be a W-wire circuit and g be a gate in_ C _computing a function f with domain_ \(D=\Sigma^I\) _for_ \(I\subseteq[W]\) _that is assigned heat function Q. The_ entropy production EP_<sub>g</sub> of g on distribution_<sup>23</sup> D _over_ \(\Sigma^W\) _is given by:_

\(\mathsf{EP}_g(\mathcal{D})=\mathcal{S}(f_\uparrow(\mathcal{D}))-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D})+\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[Q(x_I)]\)

Note \(\mathcal{S}(f_\uparrow(\mathcal{D}))\) is used in Definition 2.24 instead of S(_f_(D)) since D is a distribution on all _W_ wires. Note that \(\mathcal{S}(f_\uparrow(\mathcal{D}))-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D})\) is the _negation_ of the Landauer cost of _f_ on D (Definition 2.19), thus is nonpositive by Definition 2.5. E<sub>_x_∼D</sub>\[_Q(x<sub>I</sub>_)\] is the _entropy flow/heat released_ (see Section 1 for discussion of this term in the broader field of stochastic thermodynamics) in the context of circuits that exchange heat with the environment through their gates.

It is necessary to define EP_<sub>g</sub>_ in the context of the larger circuit, since \(\mathcal{S}(f_\uparrow(\mathcal{D}))-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D})\) is a global property of the circuit, while E<sub>_x_∼D</sub>\[_Q(x<sub>I</sub>_)\] is a property of the marginal distribution of D on the coordinates in _I_. We can also define a local equivalent, termed \(\mathsf{EP}_g^\mathsf{Loc}\), to EP_<sub>g</sub>_, which gives a lower bound on the actual entropy production EP_<sub>g</sub>_. In Appendix D we show how these two quantities are related (Proposition D.1).

**Definition 2.25** (local gate entropy production)**.** _Let g be a gate computing a function f with domain D that is assigned a heat function Q. The_ local entropy production \(\mathsf{EP}_g^\mathsf{Loc}\) _of g on input distribution_ D _over D is given by:_

\(\mathsf{EP}_g^\mathsf{Loc}(\mathcal{D})=\mathcal{S}(f(\mathcal{D}))-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D})+\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}[Q(x)].\)

We are ultimately interested in characterizing the entropy production of a circuit. When a circuit receives some distribution D over its inputs, this could in principal be a marginal distribution where the circuit’s inputs are only a subset of the variables in a larger system, with which the inputs may have mutual information that would call for different heat functions for "globally optimal" heat release for each gate. We give the following definition for the entropy production of a circuit under the assumption that its input distribution D is independent from the outside world.

**Definition 2.26** (circuit entropy production)**.** _Let_ C _be a thermodynamic circuit with gates_ \(g\in G\) _that cleanly computes a function f with domain D. Let_ D _be a distribution over D and_ D_<sub>g</sub> be the induced marginal distribution over inputs for gate g which has heat function Q<sub>g</sub>. The_ circuit entropy production _of_ C _on distribution_ D _is given by_

\(\mathsf{EP}_\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{D})=\mathcal{S}(f(\mathcal{D}))-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D})+\sum_{g\in G}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_g}[Q_g(x)]\)

<sup>23</sup>Note D is not the input distribution to the whole circuit, but the induced distribution on all _W_ wires _just prior_ to applying gate _g_.

<tbc>EP<sub>C</sub>(D) as defined above is a lower bound on the actual entropy production involved with running the circuit, as we show in Appendix D (Proposition D.1). This bound is tight when D is an independent source of randomness uncorrelated with the rest of the universe. We call this circuit entropy production because it is exactly the entropy production of the circuit as if it were isolated from its environment. We note that this is the same notion of entropy production for circuits used in prior works (i.e., \[WK20, YCW26, YYW26\]).

**Remark 2.27.** _We have defined_ 3 _separate types of entropy production in this section. Informally,_ \(\mathsf{EP}_g^\mathsf{Loc}\) _is the entropy production due to using a sub-optimal heat function for gate g given its induced marginal distribution over inputs. This captures what the entropy production of g would be if its input distribution_ D _were sampled independently of the rest of the universe._ EP_<sub>g</sub>, which is always at least_ \(\mathsf{EP}_g^\mathsf{Loc}\)_, captures_ \(\mathsf{EP}_g^\mathsf{Loc}\) _plus additional costs due to_ D _having correlations with other wires in the circuit. Finally_ EP<sub>C</sub> _is the total entropy production across all gates in the circuit under the assumption that_ D _is sampled independently from the rest of the universe. We will be proving lower and upper bounds on_ EP<sub>C</sub> _throughout the body this paper and we use both_ EP_<sub>g</sub> and_ \(\mathsf{EP}_g^\mathsf{Loc}\) _primarily in Appendices C and D where we discuss mismatch costs._

## Overwriting circuits.

It is worth noting that in \[YCW26, YYW26\] the authors use a different notion of a thermodynamic circuit than we consider here. In their _overwriting_ model, a circuit is defined (as is common in most non-quantum circuit complexity classes) as a DAG where the nodes are labeled with gates and the in-edges define the inputs for each gate. The authors are interested in repeated runs of their circuit where the old logical configuration of each gate is overwritten one gate at a time during the next run, so the thermodynamic costs are incurred incrementally as each gate is updated and replaces its old output with the new one. The overwriting model is an accurate abstraction of the CMOS architecture; however, it places some restrictions on what is feasible with circuits from a theoretical perspective. For example a logically reversible gate in the our circuit model admits the valid heat function _Q(x_)=0 on all inputs. In the overwriting model, this gate must release heat when run on independently distributed inputs unless it is computing a constant function.<sup>24</sup> In fact, we can see that any circuit in the overwriting model can be simulated in our circuit model, simulating a _k_-input, 1-output gate by using _k_ ‘input’ wires and one ‘output’ wire in each of our gates, setting the other _k_-1 wires to 0. Each gate in the simulated overwriting circuit is now a gate in our circuit model that treats the output wires of its parents (or the input) as read-only inputs and only modifies its own output wire. At the end of the computation, the values stored in all output wires for intermediate gates are erased.<sup>25</sup>

## 3 Deriving optimal heat functions

Now we show how to derive the optimal heat function for a known distribution over inputs. Recall that for a logically reversible operation, i.e., computing an injective function \(f:D\rightarrow R\), an optimal heat function is 0 on all inputs. In this case, no matter the input distribution D, since each input _x_ maps to its own unique output _f(x_), Pr<sub>_f_(D)</sub>\[_f(x_)\]=Pr<sub>D</sub>\[_x_\], thus \(log\left(Pr_{f(\mathcal{D})}[f(x)]/Pr_\mathcal{D}[x]\right)=0\). If _f_ is not injective, it remains the case that any input _x_ mapping to its own unique output _f(x_) has zero expected heat released on input _x_. "Colliding" inputs will release more heat the more inputs map to a single output (more precisely, the greater the total probability Pr<sub>_f_(D)</sub>\[_f(x_)\] of inputs _x_ sharing output _f(x_)): \(stilllog\left(Pr_{f(\mathcal{D})}[f(x)]/Pr_\mathcal{D}[x]\right)\) (now strictly positive) is the expected heat released.

## 4.1 PP-complete language for optimizing heat functions

We start with the language L<sub>_Q_-min</sub> that we will prove PP-complete.

**Definition 4.1.** L<sub>_Q_-min</sub> _is a set of tuples_ (C_,g,x,a,b_) _where_ C _is a Boolean circuit, g is a gate in that circuit, x is a potential input to that gate, and q=a/b is a positive rational number. We say that_ \((\mathcal{C},g,x,a,b)\in\mathcal{L}_{Q-\mathrm{min}}\) _if, when_ C _receives the uniform distribution over inputs, there exists some valid heat function Q for gate g that minimizes the expected heat release on its induced marginal input distribution such that_ \(Q(x)\ge\mathrm{log}q\).

There are a total of _n_ erasure gates in this circuit that erase the individual inputs and _n_-2 erasure gates that erase the partial products \(x_1\wedge x_2\) through \(x_1\wedge\dots\wedge x_{n-1}\). Since the inputs are unbiased bits, the expected heat release of these gates is H<sub>2</sub>(1/2)=1 per gate and _n_ across all gates. For the partial product erasures, the _i_’th such gate erases the value of \(x_1\wedge\dots\wedge x_{i+1}\). Again we know that the _x<sub>i</sub>_ are independently and uniformly distributed bits and therefore the _i_’th partial erasure gate is erasing a bit that has the value 1 with probability 2<sup>-_i_-1</sup>. The expected heat release for this gate is therefore H<sub>2</sub>(2<sup>-_i_-1</sup>). Thus our total expected heat release for the circuit is \(n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-2}\mathrm{H}_2(2^{-i-1})\). Since we have the same overall mapping of inputs to outputs as the binary tree case, our change in entropy is H<sub>2</sub>(2<sup>-_n_</sup>)-_n_. This gives us a circuit entropy production of

\(\mathsf{EP}_\mathcal{C}=(\mathrm{H}_2(2^{-n})-n)+n+\sum_{i=1}^{n-2}\mathrm{H}_2(2^{-i-1})=\sum_{i=2}^n\mathrm{H}_2(2^{-i})\le\sum_{i=2}^n2^{-i}(i+\mathrm{log}(e))\le(3+\mathrm{log}(e))/2\)

which is _O_(1).

Another way one could compute the circuit entropy production of these circuits would be to use Proposition D.1 and sum up the drops of mutual information associated with executing each gate. Since the gates we are considering here are each locally optimal, this would give us the same values of EP<sub>C</sub> that we computed here. Doing so is the primary approach used in prior works (i.e. [YYW26]) to produce lower bounds on the local entropy production of circuits. By using heat functions, we can exactly compute the circuit entropy production by only analyzing the local behavior of the individual gates. This lets us ignore more global properties of the circuit like the drops in mutual information, making our approach better suited to analyzing complex circuits where these mutual information terms are hard to quantify.

## 5.2 Batcher’s odd-even mergesort network

We now give bounds on the circuit entropy production of Batcher’s odd-even mergesort network [Bat68]. We note that the Landauer cost of a sorting network acting on bits chosen uniformly<tbc>

at random is \(\Omega(n)\), since for an input with exactly _k≈n/_20’s, it collapses \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{k}\ge(n/k)^k\) different inputs to the single output 0_<sup>k</sup>_1<sup>_n-k_</sup>. As a result, by Proposition 2.20 applied to the whole circuit, any sorting network necessarily releases heat at least \(\Omega(n)\). In this section we show that the Batcher network gates can be assigned heat functions meeting this bound on heat released: _O(n_) (Theorem 5.2). It remains an open question whether entropy production is necessarily \(\Omega(n)\) in any sorting network but we are able to show that the Batcher’s odd-even mergesort network on binary inputs does have cost \(\Omega(n)\) (Theorem 5.4). We then turn to the integer case, where the Landauer cost (i.e. drop in entropy) of a sorting network acting on a uniformly random permutation of {0,1_,...,n_-1} is \(\Theta(nlogn)\). In Theorem 5.18 we leverage a sorting network of Leighton and Plaxton \[LP98\], to obtain a sorting network with size \(\Theta(nlog^2n)\) but only \(\Theta(nlogn)\) heat dissipation. In contrast, by generalizing to a sorting circuit with more than _n_ wires, it _is_ possible to achieve zero circuit entropy production; see Section 6.1.

## 5.2.1 Binary inputs

We first consider the case where the input to be sorted is a length _n_ bitstring selected uniformly at random. It is known that the correctness of a sorting network can be determined by only checking its behavior on such inputs.

**Proposition 5.1** (\[Knu98\])**.** _A sorting network on n inputs from any ordered set is correct iff it correctly sorts all inputs in_ {0,1}_<sup>n</sup>._

The binary input restriction allows for comparator gates to be implemented in a more thermodynamically efficient way. This is because the inputs (0,0) and (1,1) are the unique pre-images of outputs (0,0) and (1,1) respectively, meaning that we can set _Q_(0,0)=_Q_(1,1)=0 and we only need to optimize the values of _Q_(0,1) versus _Q_(1,0) which both map to output (0,1).

**Theorem 5.2.** _When given the uniform distribution over input x in_ {0,1}_<sup>n</sup>, there is an assignment of heat function to every gate that results in the circuit releasing only O(n_) _expected heat across all gates. Moreover, the construction need only use_ 2log(_n_)+1 _distinct heat functions._

_Proof._ We start by bounding the expected heat released in each layer of the non-recursive merge step. We will use three different types of heat functions in this construction. _Q_<sup>unif</sup> is defined such that _Q_<sup>unif</sup>(_x<sub>i</sub>,x<sub>j</sub>_)=0 when _x<sub>i</sub>=x<sub>j</sub>_ and _Q_<sup>unif</sup>(_x<sub>i</sub>,x<sub>j</sub>_)=1 when \(x_i\neq x_j\). This is an unbiased heat function that we will use either when inputs (0,0) and (1,1) are overwhelmingly common or when the number of gates in a group is sufficiently small. This heat function has the advantage that neither input (0,1) or input (1,0) releases too much heat in expectation. We also define \(Q_\varepsilon^{(0,1)}\) parameterized by \(\varepsilon\le 1/2\) such that \(Q_\varepsilon^{(0,1)}(0,0)=Q_\varepsilon^{(0,1)}(1,1)=0\), \(Q_\varepsilon^{(0,1)}(0,1)=log(1/(1-\varepsilon))\), and \(Q_\varepsilon^{(0,1)}(1,0)=log(1/\varepsilon)\). Intuitively, these functions are used to reduce the expected heat released by gates where the first input is heavily biased towards input 0 while the second input is heavily biased towards input 1. In particular, if a gate receives a marginal induced input distribution where the probability of input (1,0) is at most \(\varepsilon\le 1/2\), then the expected heat released by this gate is at most \((1-\varepsilon)log(1/(1-\varepsilon))+\varepsilon log(1/\varepsilon)\le 2\varepsilon log(1/\varepsilon)\). Likewise we define \(Q_\varepsilon^{(1,0)}\) such that \(Q_\varepsilon^{(1,0)}(a,b)=Q_\varepsilon^{(0,1)}(b,a)\) for \(\varepsilon\le 1/2\). These gates are used when the first input is heavily biased towards 1 while the second input is heavily biased towards 0. By the same reasoning as \(Q_\varepsilon^{(0,1)}\), if a<tbc>

## Layer 1

In this layer, we have that \(2^{k_\ell}=n/2\). The _upper region_ contains all gates with \(i\in\left[0,(n-n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/4\right]\) and uses the heat function _Q_<sup>unif</sup>. Since we know that \(w_0(0)\le\dots\le w_{n/2-1}(0)\) and \(w_{n/2}(0)\le\dots\le w_{n-1}(0)\) and the input was distributed uniformly at random, Proposition 2.14 gives us that the probability that _w<sub>i</sub>_(0)=1 as well as the probability that _w_<sub>_i+n/_2</sub>(0)=1 are each at most \(e^{-n^\alpha/4}\). Thus by a union bound, the probability that gate (_i,i+n/_2) receives input (0,0) is at least \(1-2\cdot e^{-n^\alpha/4}\) and so the expected released heat by every such gate is at most \(2e^{-n^\alpha/4}\).

The _middle narrow band_ contains all gates with \(i\in\left[(n-n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/4,(n+n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/4\right]\) and uses the heat function _Q_<sup>unif</sup>. There are a total of \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2+1\) gates in this band that each release at most 1 expected heat.

The _lower region_ contains all gates with \(i\in\left[(n+n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/4,n/2-1\right]\) and uses the heat function _Q_<sup>unif</sup>. Using a symmetrical argument to the upper region case, Proposition 2.14 gives us that the expected released heat of every gate in this region is at most \(2e^{-n^\alpha/4}\).

Putting all of this together, the heat released in the first layer is at most \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2+2ne^{-n^\alpha/4}+1\).

## Layer 2

In this layer, we have that \(2^{k_\ell}=n/4\). The _upper narrow band_ contains all gates with \(i\in\left[n/4,(n+n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/4\right]\) and uses the heat function _Q_<sup>unif</sup>. There are at most \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/4+1\) gates in this band that each only release at most 1 expected heat.

The _middle region_ contains all gates with \(i\in\left[(n+n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/4,(n-n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/2\right]\) and uses the heat function \(Q_\varepsilon^{(1,0)}\) for some \(\varepsilon\le 1/2\) specified later. By the construction of Batcher’s odd-even mergesort, we know that _w_<sub>_i+n/_4</sub>(1)=max(_w_<sub>_i+n/_4</sub>(0)_,w_<sub>_i-n/_4</sub>(0)). Thus, by Proposition 2.14, the probability that _w_<sub>_i+n/_4</sub>(1)=1 is at most the probability that _w_<sub>_i+n/_4</sub>(0)=1 or _w_<sub>_i-n/_4</sub>(0)=1 which is at most \(2e^{-n^\alpha/4}\). Thus the probability each gate in this region receives the input (0,1) is also at most \(2e^{-n^\alpha/4}\). Picking \(\varepsilon=2e^{-n^\alpha/4}\) and \(\alpha=1/2\) gives us that \(\varepsilon\le 1/2\) and thus the expected heat released by any gate in this region is at most \(log(e)e^{-n^\alpha/4}n^\alpha\).

The _bottom narrow band_ contains all gates with \(i\in[(n-n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/2,n/2-1]\) and uses the heat function _Q_<sup>unif</sup>. There are only \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2\) gates in this band that each only release at most 1 expected heat.

Putting all of this together, the heat released in the second layer is at most \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2+log(e)e^{-n^\alpha/4}n^{1+\alpha}+1\).

## Layer 3 and beyond

The following claim gives us that, after layer 2, most 0’s are already in the top half of wires and most 1’s are already in the bottom half of wires.

**Claim 5.3.** _Let_ \(\alpha\in(0,1)\)_. Except with probability_ \(3ne^{-n^\alpha/4}/2\)_, the following hold for every_ \(\ell\ge 2\):<tbc>

1. _The number of i such that i\<n/_2 _and_ \(w_i(\ell)=1\) _is at most_ \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2\).<tbc>

_2._ _The number of i such that_ \(i\ge n/2\) _and_ \(w_i(\ell)=0\) _is at most_ \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2\).

_Proof._ We start by proving this for \(\ell=2\).

For _i\<n/_4, _w<sub>i</sub>_(2)=_w<sub>i</sub>_(1)=min(_w<sub>i</sub>_(0)_,w_<sub>_i+n/_2</sub>(0)). We have already established using Proposition 2.14 that when \(i\le(n-n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/4\), each _w<sub>i</sub>_(0)=0 except with probability at most \(e^{-n^\alpha/4}\). By a union bound, the probability that there exists such an _i_ with _w<sub>i</sub>_(2)=1 is at most \(ne^{-n^\alpha/4}/4\). We give no bounds on the values of _w<sub>i</sub>_(2)=_w<sub>i</sub>_(1) for \(i\in[(n-n^{(1+\alpha)/2})/4,n/4-1]\), but we note that there are only \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/4\) such wires.

For \(i\in[n/4,n/2-1]\), \(w_i(2)=min(w_i(1),w_{i+n/4}(1))=min(w_i(1),max(w_{i+n/4}(0),w_{i-n/4}(0)))\). Again we have already established using Proposition 2.14 that, when \(i\in[n/4,n/2-n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/4]\), both _w_<sub>_i+n/_4</sub>(0) and _w_<sub>_i-n/_4</sub>(0) each equal 0 except with probability at most \(e^{-n^\alpha/4}\). Thus by a union bound, their max is 0 except with probability at most \(2e^{-n^\alpha/4}\). By a union bound, the probability that there exists such an _i_ with _w<sub>i</sub>_(2)=1 is at most \(ne^{-n^\alpha/4}/2\). We give no bounds on the values of _w<sub>i</sub>_(2) when \(i\in[n/2-n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/4,n/2-1]\), but we again note that there are only \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/4\) such wires.

For \(i\in[n/2,n-1]\) the proof is symmetric. By a union bound, the total failure probability across both halves of the argument is at most \(3ne^{-n^\alpha/4}/2\) and we have excluded only \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2\) wires from each half of the analysis. Note that after applying each comparator gate, the number of 1’s in the first _n/_2 wires can only decrease while the number of 1’s in the last _n/_2 wires can only increase. Thus the bound will automatically extend to all \(\ell>2\).

Next, we partition the gates in layer \(\ell\ge 3\) into three groups each. The _upper gates_ are \((i,i+2^{k_\ell})\) such that \(i+2^{k_\ell}<n/2\) and they will use the heat function _Q_<sup>unif</sup>. By Claim 5.3, except with probability \(3ne^{-n^\alpha/4}/2\), at most \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2\) upper gates receive an input other than (0,0). Thus, except with probability at most \(3ne^{-n^\alpha/4}/2\), the upper gates collectively release at most \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2\) expected heat. With probability at most \(3ne^{-n^\alpha/4}/2\), every upper gate releases at most 1 heat. Since there are at most _n/_2 such gates in a layer, the expected heat released by all upper gates is at most \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2+3n^2e^{-n^\alpha/4}/4\).

The _lower gates_ are \((i,i+2^{k_\ell})\) such that \(i\ge n/2\) and they will use the heat function _Q_<sup>unif</sup>. The reasoning is symmetric to the upper gates, so we get that the expected heat released by all lower gates is also at most \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2+3n^2e^{-n^\alpha/4}/4\).

The _crossover gates_ are \((i,i+2^{k_\ell})\) where _i\<n/_2 but \(i+2^{k_\ell}\ge n/2\) and they will use the heat function \(Q_\varepsilon^{(0,1)}\) for some \(\varepsilon\le 1/2\) that we will specify later. By Claim 5.3, except with probability \(3ne^{-n^\alpha/4}/2\), there are at most \(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}/2\) crossover gates that receive the input (1,0). When this is the case, the expected heat released by all _\<n_ such gates is less than \(nlog(1/(1-\varepsilon))+n^{(1+\alpha)/2}log(1/\varepsilon)/2\). When this is not the case, there are _\<n_ gates that each release at most \(log(1/\varepsilon)\) expected heat. Thus the overall expected heat released by the crossover gates is less than \(nlog(1/(1-\varepsilon))+n^{(1+\alpha)/2}log(1/\varepsilon)/2+3n^2e^{-n^\alpha/4}log(1/\varepsilon)/2\le 2log(e)\varepsilon n+n^{(1+\alpha)/2}log(1/\varepsilon)/2+3n^2e^{-n^\alpha/4}log(1/\varepsilon)/2\).
