Thus, in total, the expected heat released in each layer \(\ell\ge 3\) is less than \((log(n^{(1-\alpha)/2})/2+4log(e))n^{(1+\alpha)/2}+(log(n^{(1-\alpha)/2})+1)3n^2e^{-n^\alpha/4}/2\).

## Putting it all together

The total expected heat released in layers 1 and 2 is \(O(n^{(1+\alpha)/2})\) while the total for layers \(\ell\ge 3\) are each \(O(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}\mathrm{log}(n))\), which gives a total of \(O(n^{(1+\alpha)/2}\mathrm{log}^2n)\) across all non-recursive layers. Fixing our choice of \(\alpha=1/2\) makes this expression _O(n_<sup>3/4</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_n_). Since layer 0 is two recursive calls on the halves of the input, we have that if _Q(n_) is the heat released for inputs of size _n_, then _Q(n_)=2_Q(n/_2)+_O(n_<sup>3/4</sup>log<sup>2</sup>_n_) for all \(n\ge 32\). When _n\<_32 we use _Q_<sup>unif</sup> for all gates and, since the number of gates in this circuit is constant, we also get a constant upper bound for the expected heat released in this base case. Since the last term in the recursive case is sub-linear, the master theorem gives us that _Q(n_) is _O(n_). We use heat function _Q_<sup>unif</sup> across all recursive calls and we use both \(Q_\varepsilon^{(0,1)}\) and \(Q_\varepsilon^{(1,0)}\) for at most 1 unique value of \(\varepsilon\) each per recursive call. Thus there are at most 2log(_n_)+1 unique heat functions used in this construction.

In Theorem B.1 of the appendix, we give a similar proof showing that in the overwriting circuit model (see Section 2), Batcher’s sorting network can still be implemented with only _O(n_) total expected heat released.

The bound in Theorem 5.2 is asymptotically tight. We can show that the circuit entropy production of sorting _n_ bits is also \(\Omega(n)\).

**Theorem 5.4.** _When given the uniform distribution over inputs in_ {0,1}_<sup>n</sup>, for any choice of valid heat functions for each gate in Batcher’s odd-even mergesort, the circuit entropy production is_ \(\Omega(n)\).

_Proof._ We show that each base case of sorting _n_=4 inputs has constant circuit entropy production. Since this base case occurs _n/_4 times in the overall sorting network and circuit entropy production is always non-negative, the entropy production of the entire circuit must be \(\Omega(n)\). We now analyze the _n_=4 sorting network, as shown in Figure 3, on the uniform distribution over inputs. The two gates in the first layer each receive inputs 00,01,10, and 11 with probability 1/4. By Lemma 3.1 this means that the expected heat release of each of these gates when given the optimal heat function is 1/2 and the expected heat released in the first layer is 1. After the first layer, the first and third wires independently have value 1 with probability 1/4 each while the second and fourth wires independently have value 0 with probability 1/4 each. Thus by Lemma 3.1 we get that the expected heat release of these gates when given the optimal heat function is 3/8 and and the expected heat release in the second layer is 3/4. The final gate is a bit more tricky to analyze. Looking at all 16 possible inputs to the circuit, this gate receives input 00 on all inputs to the circuit with 3 or more 0’s. Likewise the gate receives input 11 on all inputs to the circuit with 3 or more 1’s. The gate receives input 01 on inputs 0011 and inputs 1100 to the circuit while the gate receives input 10 on each of the four remaining inputs with 2 zeroes and 2 ones to the circuit. Thus by Lemma 3.1 the expected heat release of this gate is (3/8)H<sub>2</sub>(1/3). Putting all of this together, the expected heat release of a 4 input sorting networks is 7/4+(3/8)H<sub>2</sub>(1/3). Meanwhile the circuit maps a uniformly random length 4 bit-string to a binomial distribution on 4 unbiased coin flips. The entropy of this output equals

\((2\mathrm{log}(16)+8\mathrm{log}(4)+6\mathrm{log}(8/3))/16=(8+16+18+6\mathrm{log}(1/3))/16=21/8-(3/8)\mathrm{log}(3)\)

and so the drop in entropy is 4-(21/8-(3/8)log(3))=11/8+(3/8)log(3). Since the released heat is 7/4+(3/8)H<sub>2</sub>(1/3), the circuit entropy production of the 4 input Batcher’s sorting network with optimal heat function is at precisely 1/8. Since the general Batcher’s odd-even mergesort network features this sub-circuit on this input distribution _n/_4 times, the overall circuit entropy production of the network is at least _n/_32 which is \(\Omega(n)\).

Next we state the key technical lemma that we will need to prove our lower bound on EP<sub>C</sub>. We need the following definition of _central gates_ in order to state our key lemma, and will use the definition of the hypergeometric distribution in the proof:

**Definition 5.9.** _We say a gate_ \((i,i+2^{k_\ell})\in G_\ell\) _is_ central _if_ \(\frac{3n}{8}\le i\le\frac{5n}{8}\) .

**Definition 5.10.** _Let_ \(HG_n^{N,K}[k]\) _denote the probability that when n items are taken without replacement from a set of N items of which exactly K are marked that exactly k marked items are taken. This is given by the hypergeometric distribution:_

\(HG_n^{N,K}[k]=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N-K}{n-k}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{K}{k}/\genfrac(){pt}{2}{N}{n},\)

_which has mean nK/N. The distribution may have one or two modes, which differ by at most 1 from the mean._

**Lemma 5.11.** _Let n be a sufficiently large power of two and_ \(\ell>\left\lceil\frac{1}{2}logn\right\rceil+1\) _be a layer in Batcher’s odd-even mergesort on n inputs. Let_ \(g=(i,i+2^{k_\ell})\in G_\ell\) _be a central gate and_ D _be the marginal distribution over input pairs_ (_x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>) _to g induced by giving the sorting network a uniformly random permutation of the set_ \[_n_\] _as input. Then there is some constant_ \(\alpha>1\) _(independent of n) such that for every_ \((x_1,x_2)\in\mathrm{supp}(\mathcal{D})\),

\(\frac{1}{\alpha}\le\frac{\mathrm{Pr}_\mathcal{D}[(x_2,x_1)]}{\mathrm{Pr}_\mathcal{D}[(x_1,x_2)]}\le\alpha.\)

Before we more formally prove this lemma, we give a detailed and more intuitive outline of the strategy. We want to show that if there are _k_ permutations of \[_n_\] resulting in a gate \(g=(i,i+2^{k_\ell})\) receiving any feasible input _x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>, then there must be at least \(k/\alpha\) permutations of \[_n_\] resulting in _g_ receiving input _x_<sub>2</sub>_,x_<sub>1</sub>. To prove this, we first note that due to the structure of Batcher’s odd even mergesort, if \(r\equiv i(\mathrm{mod}2^{k_\ell})\) then the top wire inputs to _g_ will have some fixed rank _t_ among the values of all wires after layer zero (the recursive step, which separately sorts the first and second half of the inputs independently) whose indices are congruent to \(r\mathrm{mod}2^{k_\ell}\), and bottom wire inputs to _g_ will have rank _t_+1 among the values of all wires after layer zero whose indices are congruent to \(r\mathrm{mod}2^{k_\ell+1}\). This observation is an immediate consequence of Proposition 5.7. We call these sets O and E respectively, since they correspond to indices _r_ plus either odd or even multiples of \(2^{k_\ell}\) respectively.

With this, we now know that the top input to _g_ is always the _t_’th ranked element of O while the bottom input to _g_ is always the _t_+1’st ranked element of E. To prove our lemma, it is sufficient to show that the number of permutations of \[_n_\] that lead to _x_<sub>1</sub> being the _t_’th ranked element of O and _x_<sub>2</sub> being the _t_+1’st ranked element of E is within a factor of \(\alpha\) of the number of permutations resulting in _x_<sub>2</sub> being the _t_’th ranked element of O and _x_<sub>1</sub> being the _t_+1’st ranked element of E.

Unfortunately, this is complicated by the fact that the indices of elements after layer zero (and hence our sets O and E) are the result of independently sorting the first half and the second half of the input. Thus the sets O and E are determined entirely by which inputs started on which half of the wires. We introduce sets _A_ and _B_ containing the values stored on the first and second half of the wires at the beginning of the circuit respectively. Note that, for the uniformly random permutation of \[_n_\] as input, the induced equipartition of \[_n_\] into _A_ and _B_ is selected uniformly at random. Then the sets O and E are entirely determined by _A_ and _B_.

Let _x_<sub>min</sub> and _x_<sub>max</sub> be the smaller and larger values respectively among _x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>. We observe that shifting exactly \(2^{k_\ell}\) elements from _A_ to _B_ (or from _B_ to _A_) that are smaller than _x_<sub>min</sub> and moving \(2^{k_\ell}\) elements larger than _x_<sub>max</sub> back results in flipping the sets \(\mathcal{O}\cap[x_\mathrm{min},x_\mathrm{max}]\) and \(\mathcal{E}\cap[x_\mathrm{min},x_\mathrm{max}]\), which has the effect of swapping the order of the two inputs to _g_. Moreover for any _A_ and _B_ resulting in _g_ receiving input _x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>, swapping any number of elements smaller than _x_<sub>min</sub> between _A_ and _B_ and doing likewise with elements larger than _x_<sub>max</sub> will maintain the fact that _g_ receives input _x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>. Thus we want to compare the number of possible _A_ with _s_ elements smaller than _x_<sub>min</sub> and a fixed subset _I_ of {_x_<sub>min</sub>_,...,x_<sub>max</sub>} in _A_ with the number of possible \(A'\) with \(s\pm 2^{k_\ell}\) elements smaller than _x_<sub>min</sub> and the same fixed subset of _I_ in \(A'\). The remainder of the proof is a (somewhat cumbersome) argument that these values are within a factor of \(\alpha\) of one another.

We use \(\mathcal{A}_I^s\) to denote the set of all _A_ that have \(A\cap\{x_\mathrm{min},\dots,x_\mathrm{max}\}=I\) and exactly _s_ elements smaller than _x_<sub>min</sub> in _A_. The relative size of these sets for different values of _s_ are hyper-geometrically distributed; the ‘marked’ items are elements smaller than _x_<sub>min</sub> and we want to count how many of them end up in set _A_. Since the probability mass function of the hyper-geometric distribution starts off monotonically non-decreasing until hitting some mode _s_<sup>∗</sup> and then is monotonically non-increasing, we immediately have that when \(|s-s^*|>2^{k_\ell}\) it must be the case that \(|\mathcal{A}_I^s|\le\mathrm{max}(\left|\mathcal{A}_I^{s-2^{k_\ell}}\right|,\left|\mathcal{A}_I^{s+2^{k_\ell}}\right|)\) and we are done.

When \(|s-s^*|<2^{k_\ell}\) the analysis is more involved. We show that the ratio of the squared geometric mean of \(\left|\mathcal{A}_I^{s-2^{k_\ell}}\right|\) and \(\left|\mathcal{A}_I^{s+2^{k_\ell}}\right|\) to the value of \(|\mathcal{A}_I^s|^2\) is at least some constant, \(1/\alpha^2\), by expressing \(\left|\mathcal{A}_I^{s-2^{k_\ell}}\right|\left|\mathcal{A}_I^{s+2^{k_\ell}}\right|/\left|\mathcal{A}_I^s\right|^2\) as a telescoping product. With this lower bound in hand, we can use the arithmetic, geometric mean inequality to deduce that \(\left|\mathcal{A}_I^{s-2^{k_\ell}}\right|+\left|\mathcal{A}_I^{s+2^{k_\ell}}\right|\ge|\mathcal{A}_I^s|\left(2/\alpha\right)\). This in turn gives us that if _C(a,b_) is the number of choices for _A_ resulting in _g_ receiving input _a,b_ then we always have that \(1/\alpha\le\frac{C(x_2,x_1)}{C(x_1,x_2)}\le\alpha\) as desired.

## 7 Conclusion

In this paper we posit that the concepts of entropy production and heat release provide a principled foundation for understanding inherent energy costs of computations. We introduce a thermodynamic logic circuit model in which gates (e.g., Boolean logic gates or comparator gates) are augmented with heat functions, which determine a circuit’s entropy flow and entropy production with respect to a given input distribution. We show that in general, determining optimal heat functions is computationally intractable. In contrast, we show that for specific problems (i.e. sorting) our model can be used both to analyze the thermodynamic costs of existing circuits and to design new circuits that are thermodynamically efficient.

There are many directions for future work. Our analysis of Batcher’s odd-even mergesort on bits uses a set of gate heat functions that scales with the circuit size; what are the penalties for using only a constant number of distinct heat functions for this problem? How can we analyze heat dissipation of circuits in other problem domains, such as graph algorithms? What are good general design principles for energy-efficient computation?

Theorem 6.1 shows a zero EP circuit for bit-compaction, the problem of sorting 1-bit keys with _m_-bit payloads, using _O(n_log_n_) depth (as long as log_m_ is _O(n_)). Can we design a zero EP compaction circuit with polylog(_n_) depth? This rules out erasing key bits one at a time as we do, which requires \(\Omega(n)\) depth.<sup>43</sup> Is it possible to show a lower bound of \(\Omega(n)\) depth for the clean compaction problem, arguing that zero EP erasure with constant arity gates must do so sequentially?

Another limitation of our technique to do compaction in Theorem 6.1 is that we require \(\Omega(n^2)\) erasure gates. This is necessary given our specific erasure technique: we get the circuit to a point where it has the intended output (compacted key-payload records), as well as the uncompacted keys \(b\in\{0,1\}^n\), and we erase each key bit one at a time. There are \(\Omega(n^2)\) conditional probabilities that are possible for each bit to be a 1 across all stages during this process, necessitating \(\Omega(n^2)\) erasure gates. However, this does not rule out a more sophisticated way to erase the bits in which we do not encounter so many different conditional probabilities. Perhaps some efficient reversible circuit computation could be done on _b_ to transform it into a different bit string \(b'\) of length _O(n_), such that while erasing the bits of \(b'\) in order, each bit would only have one of, say, _O_(log_n_) different (possibly position-dependent) probabilities. In this case _O(n_log_n_) total erasure gates would suffice to erase all bits.

Suppose the number of erasure gates could be reduced to _O(n_polylog(_n_)), or if \(m\gg n\) so that the _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) erasure gates are negligible. (To simplify discussion below assume _m=O_(1), so that<tbc>

Rather than insisting on EP=0, one can ask for the minimum EP achievable by compaction circuits of near-linear size or polylogarithmic depth. We know of no lower bound of the form "depth _d_ forces \(\mathsf{EP}\ge g(n,d)\)" for any _g\>_0; such a bound would be the first general quantitative trade-off between a standard circuit resource and entropy production.

Theorem 6.1 uses a single circuit, with finitely many heat functions, that has zero EP for every exchangeable input distribution simultaneously, because the conditional probability that each erased bit is 1 depends only on exchangeability. For which other classes of distributions is this possible? If, for instance, the keys are independent but position-dependent, the conditional probabilities depend on the bias of every position, and it is unclear whether finitely many heat functions suffice. Conversely, what is the EP of our circuit when the input is only approximately exchangeable, say as a function of a divergence between the actual distribution and the nearest exchangeable one?

Analogous questions about the gate and depth complexity for zero circuit entropy production sorting are natural. In general, a more detailed study of gate-depth-entropy tradeoffs for sorting is worthy of further investigation.

Our results concern expected EP and expected heat. What are the variance, and the worst case over inputs, of the heat released by our circuits, and is there a trade-off between the fluctuations of heat and circuit size or depth, in the spirit of the thermodynamic uncertainty relations of stochastic thermodynamics [HG20]? ## B Analyzing entropy flow in Batcher’s sorting network: overwriting model with binary inputs

Here we show that in the overwriting model, the expected heat dissipation of Batcher’s sorting network is _O(n_), matching our bound for our thermodynamic circuit model. We first describe useful heat functions for our analysis, then use these to bound the expected heat dissipation for layers 1 through log_n_ of Batcher’s network, and finish with a recurrence to bound the total heat dissipation. This proof is very similar to the one for our standard circuit model (i.e. Theorem 5.2).

### The overwriting model and its heat functions

In the overwriting model, we view a circuit as a DAG where every node represents a gate and edges indicate input dependence. Unlike in our standard circuit model, the gates in the overwriting model retain their output values in a persistent storage between runs and are not required to erase their inputs. As such, the old output to every gate must be _overwritten_ by a new value during each run of the circuit. For this section, we will be assuming that inputs to our overwriting circuit are independently and identically distributed and will use \(\tilde{Q}\) to denote heat functions for circuits in the overwriting model. If a gate in the overwriting model computes a function \(f:D\rightarrow R\), then it is actually computing the function _h(x,y_)=(_x,f(x_)) for every \(x\in D,y\in R\). As such, the possible heat functions for this gate is given by functions \(\tilde{Q}:D\times R\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) and the validity criteria matches that of Definition 2.21 when the function being computed is _h_.

Since our inputs are independently and identically distributed, there is a significantly simpler expression for the optimal heat function given by Lemma 3.1. Let D be the marginal induced distribution over inputs to our gate (including the output from the previous run), D_<sub>D</sub>_ be the marginal distribution over new input \(x\in D\), and D_<sub>R</sub>_ be the marginal distribution over the old output \(y\in R\). Then, since D is independently and identically distribution, we have that \(\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_D\otimes\mathcal{D}_R\). Thus the optimal heat function for our gate is given by:

\(\tilde{Q}(x,y)=log\frac{Pr_{x,y\sim h(\mathcal{D})}[(x,f(x))]}{Pr_{x,y\sim\mathcal{D}}[x,y]}=log\frac{Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_D}[x]}{Pr_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_D}[x]Pr_{y\sim\mathcal{D}_R}[y]}=log\frac{1}{Pr_{y\sim\mathcal{D}_R}[y]}.\)

So the optimal heat function for gates run on independently identically distributed inputs in the overwriting model is equivalent to the optimal heat function for erasing the value of _f(x_). Thus we will be specifying heat functions in the overwriting model whose only inputs are the values that are about to be overwritten.

_Proof._ Adding up the expected heat dissipation for layers 1 through log<sub>2</sub>_n_, we see that the total expected heat dissipation is<tbc>

\(O(n^{(1+\alpha)/2})+O(n^{(1+5\alpha)/2}\mathrm{log}_2n),\)

\(\mathsf{Q}(n)=2\mathsf{Q}(n/2)+O(n^{(1+5\alpha)/2}\mathrm{log}_2n)\)

and so is _O(n_) when \(\alpha<1/5\). The number of different heat functions used is _O_(1) per layer, and so is _O_(log_n_) in total for the network.

## C Re-deriving mismatch costs

In \[WK20, YCW26, YYW26\] the authors use the language of _mismatch costs_ to lower bound the entropy production of implementing gates in a Boolean circuit. Instead of explicitly defining heat functions, they start with the assumption that some distribution over inputs D<sup>∗</sup> minimizes the entropy production of the desired computation. Their main observation is that entropy production can be decomposed as the sum of a term characterizing how far the actual input distribution is from D<sup>∗</sup> and a term characterizing the inefficiencies even when using D<sup>∗</sup> as the input distribution. We start by characterizing how D<sup>∗</sup> can be derived from a given heat function.

**Lemma C.1.** _Let f be an arbitrary function with domain D and_ \(Q:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{\infty\}\) _be a valid heat function for computing f. Then any conditional input distribution_ \(\mathcal{D}_{|f^{-1}(y)}^*\) _that minimizes the entropy production of applying a gate g computing f with heat function Q must satisfy_

\(\mathcal{D}_{|f^{-1}(y)}^*=(\mathcal{G}_Q)_{|f^{-1}(y)}\)

_on all y where_ (G_<sub>Q</sub>_)<sub>|_f_<sup>-1</sup>(_y_)</sub> _is defined. If_ (G_<sub>Q</sub>_)<sub>|_f_<sup>-1</sup>(_y_)</sub> _is undefined, then all conditional input distributions have infinite entropy flow._

_Proof._ By the definition of entropy production, we have that for every _y_:<tbc>

\(\mathsf{EP}_g(\mathcal{D}_{|f^{-1}(y)})=-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_{|f^{-1}(y)})+\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{|f^{-1}(y)}}[Q(x)].\)

By Lemma 2.12, we know that (G_Q_)|_f_-1(_y_) is the distribution that minimizes this quantity. When (G_Q_)|_f_-1(_y_) is undefined, it must be the case that \(Q(x)=\infty\) for every \(x\in f^{-1}(y)\). In such cases, any distribution over these inputs must release infinite expected heat. **Corollary C.2.** _Let f be an arbitrary function with domain D and_ \(Q:D\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\cup\{\infty\}\) _be a valid heat function for computing f such that_ \(Q(x)\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) _for some_ \(x\in D\)_. There are actually some subtlety in our statement of Proposition C.3 that becomes obvious with the language of heat functions. In particular, we cannot always take D∗ to be the distribution over inputs that minimizes the entropy production. Due to Corollary C.2, we know that such a D∗ would only have support on _y_ that minimize EP_g_((G_Q_)|_f_-1(_y_)), and thus for many choices of D we will not have that \(\mathrm{supp}(f(\mathcal{D}))\subseteq\mathrm{supp}(f(\mathcal{D}^*))\). Proposition C.3 actually has a nice intuitive interpretation in terms of heat functions. The term _D_KL(D||D∗)-_D_KL(_f_(D)||_f_(D∗)) corresponds to how well suited _Q_ is for the input distribution D while E_y∼f_(D))\[EP_g_((G_Q_)|_f_-1(_y_))\] corresponds to how close _Q_ is to being optimal on the best possible distributions over the preimage of each _y_. ## D Entropy production from modularity Heat functions only consider the inputs to a specific gate to determine the corresponding heat release. Thus, they do not account for correlations between the inputs to this gate and the rest

of the circuit. This leads to a source of entropy production due to the locality of operations that are not injective. This source of entropy production was first identified in \[WK20\], where it was shown that the entropy production of applying a gate in a circuit is at least the drop in mutual information between the wires in this gate and the state of the remaining wires of the circuit. We prove essentially the same result, showing that it is an immediate consequence of the locality of valid heat functions. **Proposition D.1** (\[WK20\])**.** _Let_ C _be a thermodynamic circuit with W wires, and let X,Y be a partition of_ \[_W_\] _and_ C_t_-1\[_X_\],C_t_-1\[_Y_\]∼D_t_-1 _be random variables for the state of the wires in X,Y after applying gate t_-1 _in_ C_. Let_ D_X be the marginal distribution of random variable_ C_t_-1\[_X_\] _according to distribution_ D_t_-1_. Then if gate gt computes the function_ \(f^{g_t}:\Sigma^X\rightarrow\Sigma^X\) _and has valid heat function Qgt, the entropy production of applying gt as the next gate in_ C _is_ \(\mathsf{EP}_{g_t}^\mathsf{Loc}(\mathcal{D}_X)+\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{C}_{t-1}[X];\mathcal{C}_t[Y])-\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{C}_t[X];\mathcal{C}_t[Y])\). _Proof._ By Definition 2.25, \(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_X}[Q_{g_t}(x)]=\mathsf{EP}_{g_t}^\mathsf{Loc}(\mathcal{D}_X)+\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_{t-1}[X])-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_t[X])\) Let D_t_ be the distribution over states of the circuit after applying _gt_. Since C_t_-1\[_Y_\] is the same as C_t_\[_Y_\], we know that according to Definition 2.24: \(\mathsf{EP}_{g_t}(\mathcal{D}_{t-1})=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_{t-1}}[Q_{g_t}(x_X)]+\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_t)-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_{t-1})\)
\(=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}_X}[Q_{g_t}(x)]+\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_t)-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_{t-1})\)
\(=\mathsf{EP}_{g_t}^\mathsf{Loc}(\mathcal{D}_X)+\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_{t-1}[X])-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_t[X])+\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_t)-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{D}_{t-1})\)
\(=\mathsf{EP}_{g_t}^\mathsf{Loc}(\mathcal{D}_X)+\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_{t-1}[X])-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_t[X])+\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_t[X],\mathcal{C}_t[Y])-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_{t-1}[X],\mathcal{C}_t[Y])\)
\(=\mathsf{EP}_{g_t}^\mathsf{Loc}(\mathcal{D}_X)+\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_{t-1}[X])-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_t[X])+\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_t[X]|\mathcal{C}_t[Y])-\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{C}_{t-1}[X]|\mathcal{C}_t[Y])\)
\(=\mathsf{EP}_{g_t}^\mathsf{Loc}(\mathcal{D}_X)+\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{C}_{t-1}[X];\mathcal{C}_t[Y])-\mathcal{I}(\mathcal{C}_t[X];\mathcal{C}_t[Y])\) as desired. Thus we can decompose entropy production into a term based off of sub-optimal computation on the marginal input distribution plus the drop in mutual information caused by the locality constraint on heat functions.
